question.problem:
Consider the polar curve $r=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ for $\theta \in [0,2\pi ).$ Given that 

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta ),\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ),
$$

and ${y}^{′}(\frac{3\pi }{2})=0,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. ${x}^{′}(\frac{3\pi }{2})=0$

II. ${lim}_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\infty $

III. The curve has a vertical tangent at $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{2}$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the following results.*

$$
\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )\to {0}^{-}\,\text{as}\,\theta \to {(\frac{3\pi }{2})}^{-} \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )\to {0}^{+}\,\text{as}\,\theta \to {(\frac{3\pi }{2})}^{+}\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
For a given polar curve, there is a vertical tangent at $\theta ={\theta }_{0}$ if

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}{{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}
$$

is infinite. This means that

$$
{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})\ne 0\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})=0.
$$

However, if the curve is continuous at ${\theta }_{0}$ yet the derivative takes the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}$ at this point, we say that the curve has a vertical tangent at this point if

$$
{lim}_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\pm \infty \,\text{and}\,{lim}_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\pm \infty .
$$

In this case, we're told that ${y}^{′}(\frac{3\pi }{2})=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Substituting $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{2}$ into the expression for ${x}^{′}(\theta ),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\frac{3\pi }{2}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{3\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & =-1-(-1) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Computing the limit as $\theta \to {(\frac{3\pi }{2})}^{-}$ using L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={lim}_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )}) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}(\frac{{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))}^{′}}{{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta ))}^{′}}) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}(\frac{-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )}).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the limit in the numerator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi ) \\  & =-(-1)+2\cdot (-1) \\  & =1-2 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the first hint, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={lim}_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}(\frac{-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )}) \\  & =\frac{-1}{{0}^{-}} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Using the calculations from part II, and the second hint, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={lim}_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{+}}(\frac{-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )}) \\  & =\frac{-1}{{0}^{+}} \\  & =-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Since the limits of our derivative are both infinite, there is a vertical tangent to the curve at $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{2}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14227801/assets/f4462c7c41e7d6d5d10acec7627ac54f73477569356e22857659f5110847302d.png)

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."
